paragraphs: Conformal prediction adds uncertainty estimates to a model after training. Feature Conformal Prediction applies this idea within the model’s feature space and can produce narrower prediction bands. Its practical bottleneck comes afterward: translating those bands into the output space requires expensive nonlinear operations, making the uncertainty procedure costly to use.

Fast Feature Conformal Prediction replaces these transformations with a first-order Taylor approximation. This approximates the relevant nonlinear behavior through a local linear description, reducing the work needed to obtain output-space uncertainty estimates. The paper also introduces a new nonconformity score, the quantity used to assess how unusual an example is within the conformal procedure.

In the reported regression and classification experiments, the faster method performs comparably to Feature Conformal Prediction, and both outperform the vanilla conformal approach. Computational time falls by approximately a factor of 50. These results suggest that approximating the costly transformation can preserve the empirical benefits of feature-space prediction bands while making their computation substantially more practical.
neurips-2025-accelerating-feature-confor.tldr: A Taylor approximation makes feature-space conformal prediction about 50 times faster in reported experiments while preserving comparable performance.

paragraphs: Automated evaluators can make comparing AI models cheaper by supplying synthetic evaluations alongside real-world observations. Their judgments may reduce statistical variability, but they can also introduce bias. Prediction-powered inference corrects that bias using real observations, yet an inaccurate evaluator can still make estimation less sample-efficient than using real data alone.

R-AutoEval+ addresses this problem by adaptively controlling how much the performance estimate depends on synthetic data. Its evaluation variable changes according to the usefulness of the automated evaluator. When that evaluator is insufficiently accurate, the framework falls back to conventional evaluation, rather than continuing to rely on an unhelpful source of information.

The paper provides finite-sample reliability guarantees together with sample efficiency that is improved or at least no worse than conventional methods. Experiments examine LLM judges in quantization-setting selection, prompt design, and reasoning-budget allocation. The stated contribution is therefore both statistical and practical: synthetic judgments become an adjustable resource whose value is assessed within the evaluation procedure.
neurips-2025-adaptive-prediction-powered.tldr: R-AutoEval+ adaptively uses automated judgments to estimate model performance with reliability guarantees and sample efficiency no worse than conventional evaluation.

paragraphs: An aggregate benchmark score describes how often a model succeeds, but it gives a limited picture of which challenges remain. AGI-Elo approaches evaluation by rating both the capability of the system being tested and the difficulty of individual test cases. The framework is intended to cover AI models or humans across vision, language, and action.

Its ratings arise from competitive interactions between models and tasks. Treating task difficulty as something to estimate makes evaluation sensitive to the distribution of challenges, including difficult cases in the long tail. This supports a more detailed account of the gap between current competence and mastery of a task than a model-only summary provides.

The authors evaluate the system across multiple established datasets and models from different domains, reporting evidence of robustness and generalizability. The resulting rating distributions help interpret task difficulty, model progress, and unresolved challenges. The contribution is a shared evaluation framework for examining those relationships, rather than merely compressing performance into another aggregate score.
neurips-2025-agi-elo-how-far-are-we-from.tldr: AGI-Elo jointly rates model competence and test-case difficulty to reveal performance gaps hidden by aggregate benchmark scores.

paragraphs: Matrix quantization reduces storage by representing real-valued entries in a compact format. Conventional approaches considered here reconstruct matrices through linear combinations of binary components. Binary Quadratic Quantization, or BQQ, instead uses quadratic expressions in binary variables, giving the representation additional expressive capacity while retaining a very compact data format.

The authors test this idea on general matrix compression and on post-training quantization of pretrained Vision Transformer models. Across the matrix data examined, BQQ offers a better balance between memory use and reconstruction error than conventional methods. This evaluates whether the richer binary representation can preserve more information for a given storage budget.

The neural-network results also show strong performance without PTQ-specific binary matrix optimization. At an equivalent two-bit setting on ImageNet, the authors report improvements over a state-of-the-art PTQ method of up to 2.2% with calibration and 59.1% without data. They explicitly do not position tight-memory PTQ accuracy as their main optimization target; the broader finding concerns the effectiveness of quadratic binary representations.
neurips-2025-binary-quadratic-quantizati.tldr: BQQ uses quadratic binary expressions to improve matrix compression and delivers strong reported results when quantizing Vision Transformers.

paragraphs: Block coordinate descent trains a network by updating groups of variables in turn. Existing analyses described in this paper establish convergence to stationary points, where further improvement is not guaranteed. The authors strengthen that result for their algorithm under strictly increasing activation functions, proving convergence to global minima with arbitrarily small loss.

The analysis separates the behavior of output and hidden layers. The output-layer loss decreases exponentially, while the hidden-layer losses remain controlled. The paper also derives generalization bounds using Rademacher complexity, connecting its optimization analysis with an account of performance beyond the training data. These are distinct contributions: achieving small training loss and bounding generalization address different aspects of learning.

ReLU does not satisfy the strict monotonicity assumption, so the authors introduce a modified algorithm with skip connections and non-negative projection. They extend their convergence guarantees to that version. Experiments obtain small losses with both strictly monotonic activations and ReLU, supporting the theoretical findings for the respective algorithms rather than establishing an unrestricted guarantee for all network training.
neurips-2025-block-coordinate-descent-fo.tldr: The paper proves global convergence for a neural-network block coordinate descent algorithm under strictly increasing activations and extends the result to a modified ReLU version.

paragraphs: Diffusion transformers repeatedly compute features as generation progresses, making inference expensive. Caching methods save some of those features and reuse them at later timesteps. The paper identifies a restriction in approaches that only choose between using a cached feature unchanged and running the model again: they cannot cheaply adjust a reused feature.

The proposed framework adds selective linear modulation to feature caching. A learned gate decides when modulation should be applied, and the adjustment parameters are learned as well. The motivation is the high cosine similarity observed between features at consecutive timesteps, which suggests that a modest adjustment can be useful without requiring full recomputation.

Experiments report generation performance similar to the original sampler with substantially less computation. FLOPs and latency improve by factors of 2.93 and 2.15 for DiT-XL/2, and 2.83 and 1.50 for PixArt-alpha. Modulating as few as 2% of layers is effective in the reported tests, adding negligible overhead. The different latency and FLOP reductions also distinguish measured runtime gains from computational savings.
neurips-2025-diffusion-on-demand-selecti.tldr: Learned gates selectively adjust cached diffusion features, reducing computation and latency while retaining similar generation performance in experiments.

paragraphs: Video generators can produce convincing motion without exposing a separate representation that lets a creator transfer that motion elsewhere. DisMo learns such a representation directly from raw videos through an image reconstruction objective. Its aim is to capture motion independently of static information such as appearance, object identity, or pose.

This separation enables motion transfer between semantically unrelated entities without requiring correspondences between their objects. The paper presents the representation as a way to preserve motion semantics while following the desired content conditioning, addressing source-structure overfitting and action drift described for prior methods. Lightweight adapters connect the motion representation to video generators, allowing the motion component to be used alongside existing generation systems.

The authors demonstrate the approach on a diverse collection of motion-transfer tasks. They also evaluate whether the representation supports motion understanding, reporting stronger zero-shot action classification than state-of-the-art video representations such as V-JEPA on benchmarks including Something-Something v2 and Jester. Those results suggest that the learned separation is useful for both controlling generated motion and recognizing actions.
neurips-2025-dismo-disentangled-motion-r.tldr: DisMo learns motion representations separate from appearance, enabling cross-category motion transfer and strong zero-shot action recognition.

paragraphs: Sampling becomes difficult when a probability distribution must obey equality and inequality constraints, especially when the allowed region is nonconvex. Existing approaches discussed in the paper often require expensive projections back onto that region. They also tend to specialize in one constraint type, and rigorous quantitative convergence guarantees are often unavailable.

Overdamped Langevin with Landing, or OLLA, provides a framework for dynamics that accommodate both kinds of constraints. Alongside the stochastic sampling process, it deterministically corrects trajectories in the direction normal to the constraint surface. This correction removes the need for explicit projection steps while directing the dynamics toward the constrained target distribution.

Under suitable regularity conditions on the density and constraint set, the authors prove exponential convergence in Wasserstein-2 distance, a measure of discrepancy between distributions. Experiments compare OLLA with projection-based constrained Langevin algorithms and slack-variable variants, showing favorable computational cost and reasonable empirical mixing. The theoretical result is conditional on the stated regularity requirements, while the experiments assess how efficiently the method explores the tested distributions.
neurips-2025-fast-non-log-concave-sampli.tldr: OLLA samples under equality and inequality constraints without explicit projections and has exponential convergence guarantees under suitable regularity conditions.

paragraphs: Medical time-series interpretation requires connecting changing signals with clinical context and specialized knowledge. An LLM may supply useful knowledge from biomedical literature and clinical guidelines, but its usefulness depends on how the signals are presented. A prompt must direct attention to information that matters for clinical interpretation, including subtle indicators used in expert decision-making.

InDiGO addresses this prompt-content problem through a knowledge-aware evolutionary learning framework. It integrates clinical signals with decision-making indicators and improves that integration through iterative optimization. The central idea is to make domain knowledge part of how information is selected and organized for the language model, so that the prompt better reflects the interpretation task.

Across four medical benchmarks, the authors report that InDiGO consistently outperforms prior methods. These findings support the usefulness of optimizing the connection between measured signals and clinically meaningful indicators. The contribution concerns how medical series are translated into informative input for an LLM, helping the model bring its contextual knowledge to bear on the signals being analyzed.
neurips-2025-from-indicators-to-insights.tldr: InDiGO iteratively combines clinical signals and decision-making indicators to improve LLM-based medical time-series analysis across four benchmarks.

paragraphs: Medical image segmentation must produce coherent regions while accurately tracing fine boundaries. Maintaining both properties across image resolutions is difficult for pixel-wise decoders. GauSAM adapts the Segment Anything Model by representing segmentation masks as continuous probability fields built from learnable two-dimensional Gaussian primitives, giving smooth spatial structure a central role in the representation.

Smoothness alone does not capture every important edge, so the method also extracts directional frequency information with contourlet transforms. These provide information about boundaries and fine textures that guides where the Gaussian primitives are placed. The same high-frequency contour information also enriches the image encoder, linking boundary-sensitive features with the continuous mask representation.

Experiments across diverse two-dimensional medical segmentation tasks report robust generalization and state-of-the-art performance with 1.2 million trainable parameters. The significance is the combination of two complementary requirements: continuous fields support spatial consistency, while contour guidance helps retain detailed boundaries. The reported results indicate that this combination can adapt SAM effectively without requiring a large number of trainable parameters.
neurips-2025-gausam-contourguided-2d-gau.tldr: GauSAM combines continuous Gaussian mask fields with contour guidance to improve multiscale medical segmentation using 1.2 million trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Choosing a pretraining data mixture for one downstream task can improve that task while harming others. GRAPE addresses this tradeoff by adapting the mixture for several targets simultaneously. It adjusts both the sampling weights of source domains and the importance assigned to individual target tasks, allowing priorities to change as learning progresses.

The method formulates these two adjustments as an interleaved minimax problem. An inner step gives greater weight to tasks showing the least improvement under the current mixture, using group distributionally robust optimization. An outer step then changes the source-domain weights to improve loss reduction on those prioritized tasks. This connects what the model studies next with where its progress is weakest.

On ClimbLab and SlimPajama, the authors report consistently better reasoning accuracy than baseline methods across six benchmarks. In a multilingual setting, GRAPE also selects mixtures from mainstream languages that improve language modeling across eight low-resource target languages. Together, these findings support adaptive reweighting as a way to pursue multiple target capabilities while accounting for uneven learning progress.
neurips-2025-grape-optimize-data-mixture.tldr: GRAPE jointly adapts source-data mixtures and target-task priorities to improve performance across multiple reasoning and multilingual targets.

paragraphs: Graph prompting adapts a pretrained graph neural network by changing its input while keeping the network frozen. Many existing methods modify node features or hidden representations. GraphTOP instead focuses on the graph’s connectivity, asking whether changing which nodes are connected can make a pretrained model more useful for a downstream task.

The framework expresses this adaptation as edge rewiring within local subgraphs spanning multiple hops. Because edge choices are discrete, it uses reparameterization to move the optimization into a continuous probability space. The proposed relaxation is designed to remain tight while preserving graph sparsity, allowing topology changes to be learned without turning the graph into a densely connected structure.

Experiments cover five graph datasets and four pretraining strategies. The authors report that GraphTOP outperforms six baselines on multiple node-classification datasets. These results support connectivity as a useful target for graph prompting: a frozen network can be adapted through the relationships presented to it, extending the range of input changes available during downstream adaptation.
neurips-2025-graphtop-graph-topology-ori.tldr: GraphTOP adapts frozen graph neural networks by learning sparse local edge rewiring, outperforming six baselines in reported node-classification experiments.

paragraphs: Offline imitation learning aims to learn a good decision-making policy from recorded expert state-action pairs. Some existing theory assumes the expert belongs to a known, tractable policy class. This paper takes a different route by imposing structure on the environment’s policy-value functions, using the assumption of Q-pi realizability to support learning guarantees.

The proposed algorithm, saddle-point offline imitation learning, is called SPOIL. For linear Q-pi-realizable Markov decision processes, it is guaranteed to match any expert’s performance up to an additive error epsilon using a sample count of order epsilon to the power minus two. The result extends to possibly nonlinear realizable environments, with a worse sample requirement of order epsilon to the power minus four.

The analysis also motivates a loss function for training critic networks from expert data. On standard benchmarks, a neural implementation outperforms behavior cloning and is competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms. The paper thus connects a conditional theoretical guarantee with a practical training objective, while making clear that the stronger sample-efficiency result belongs to the linear setting.
neurips-2025-inverse-q-learning-done-rig.tldr: SPOIL provides offline imitation-learning guarantees under Q-pi realizability and motivates a critic loss with competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Private sampling seeks to generate a sample whose distribution resembles a private distribution while satisfying local differential privacy. A globally minimax sampler protects against the worst case across an entire distribution class. This paper instead studies the worst-case error near a fixed reference distribution, allowing the analysis to reflect local knowledge about the target.

The authors characterize the exact local minimax error as a function of the reference distribution and privacy level. They extend prior analysis to functional local differential privacy and show how the globally optimal sampler yields a locally optimal one when restricted to a neighborhood of the reference. They also derive a closed-form optimal sampler that does not depend on which f-divergence measures distributional error.

The reference distribution can represent public data, providing a natural setting in which local information is available without exposing private observations. In experiments motivated by this setting, the local sampler consistently outperforms global minimax samplers. The result shows how restricting the relevant distribution class can improve private sampling while retaining an explicit optimality characterization.
neurips-2025-locally-optimal-private-sam.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal private sampling near a reference distribution and shows empirical benefits when that reference represents public data.

paragraphs: Learning physical dynamics can require representing both randomness and the geometry of the space in which a system evolves. The paper identifies a gap between two approaches: Hamiltonian neural networks model conservative dynamics in flat space, while manifold diffusion models account for geometry and randomness but lack the same physical inductive structure.

Neural Hamiltonian Diffusion combines these ingredients in one framework. A neural network represents the Hamiltonian, and a stochastic differential equation defines motion on a differentiable manifold. The space has a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian geometry together with a Poisson structure, providing the mathematical ingredients for connecting the learned Hamiltonian to dynamics that respect the space’s organization.

This formulation supports physically consistent modeling in curved, periodic, and causally structured spaces. The authors demonstrate that the proposed dynamics generalize existing approaches and apply to systems ranging from molecular dynamics to relativistic many-body problems. The contribution is a unified modeling framework that accommodates geometric structure, Hamiltonian organization, and stochastic behavior within the same description of a system’s evolution.
neurips-2025-neural-hamiltonian-diffusio.tldr: Neural Hamiltonian Diffusion combines learned Hamiltonians, stochastic dynamics, and manifold geometry to model physically structured systems.

paragraphs: Assessing a language model’s answer is difficult when an API hides its internal representations. This paper uses follow-up questions to obtain an alternative representation of model behavior. The probabilities of responses to those questions become features for a predictor, allowing assessment through observable interactions rather than requiring access to hidden activations.

A linear model trained on these features predicts correctness on question-answering and reasoning benchmarks. The authors report that it can even outperform linear predictors with white-box access to model internals. This finding suggests that carefully elicited responses can expose useful behavioral information in a form that a simple predictor can use effectively.

The same approach also distinguishes clean models from versions influenced by adversarial system prompts to give incorrect answers or introduce code bugs. In another application, it differentiates between black-box models, supporting detection of misrepresented models behind an API. These results point to follow-up interactions as a promising monitoring tool across correctness assessment, behavioral manipulation detection, and model identification.
neurips-2025-predicting-the-performance-.tldr: Response probabilities from follow-up questions provide features for predicting black-box model correctness, detecting manipulation, and distinguishing model identities.

paragraphs: Quantum Visual Field, or QVF, is a quantum implicit representation for learning two-dimensional images and three-dimensional geometric fields. It addresses how classical information enters a quantum model, how the parameterized circuit is structured, and how learned signals are recovered. These choices are treated together as an architecture for representing visual information.

The method uses neural amplitude encoding based on a learnable energy manifold to embed classical data into quantum statevectors. Its circuit has a fully entangled design and performs unitary operations in a real Hilbert space, which the authors associate with numerically stable training and fast convergence. Learned signals are extracted directly through measurements, without classical post-processing of those measurements.

Experiments run on a quantum hardware simulator show better visual representation accuracy than an existing quantum approach and competitive results against widely used classical foundational baselines. Applications include completing two- and three-dimensional fields and interpolating three-dimensional shapes. These findings establish the architecture’s empirical potential in simulation while tying representation quality to its encoding, circuit, and measurement design.
neurips-2025-quantum-visual-fields-with-.tldr: QVF combines neural amplitude encoding and entangled quantum circuits to learn visual fields, with competitive representation results in simulator experiments.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning predicts how strongly several labels apply to an example. In the semi-supervised setting, predicted labels help train on unlabeled examples. The paper argues that matching an overall distribution through KL divergence alone can still produce pseudo-labels with incorrect label ordering, causing the model to learn misleading semantic relationships.

RankMatch explicitly considers relationships between label rankings when learning from labeled data, aiming to generate better pseudo-labels. It then uses those pseudo-labels flexibly: focusing on their ordering while disregarding the margins between label values helps prevent overfitting. This separates confidence in which labels rank higher from confidence in the exact numerical gaps between them.

The authors provide a theoretical result that incorporating ranking correlations improves semi-supervised label distribution learning, along with generalization error bounds for RankMatch. Real-world experiments also support its effectiveness. The central contribution is to treat relative label order as useful supervision in its own right, rather than relying entirely on agreement between numerical distributions when learning from model-generated targets.
neurips-2025-rankmatch-a-novel-approach-.tldr: RankMatch improves semi-supervised label distribution learning by preserving label rankings and avoiding overreliance on pseudo-label value gaps.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether explicitly modeling periodic structure can improve how language models learn. Its starting point is that limitations in a Transformer’s handling of periodicity may hinder learning efficiency and the extraction of underlying rules. The proposed architecture, FANformer, brings Fourier Analysis Network components into the attention mechanism to address this issue.

The change occurs in attention’s feature-projection process, giving periodicity modeling a role within the architecture itself. Language-modeling experiments compare FANformer with Transformers as both model size and training-token counts increase. The authors report consistent improvements across these scaling experiments, supporting their claim that this architectural change can make learning more efficient.

The pretrained FANformer-1B also improves downstream performance over open-source models with similar parameter counts or training-token budgets. Further experiments report stronger ability to learn and apply rules for reasoning than a Transformer. These findings support periodicity modeling as a promising architectural direction; they establish empirical benefits for the proposed design rather than an identity between periodicity and all forms of reasoning.
neurips-2025-reasoning-is-periodicity-im.tldr: FANformer adds Fourier-based periodicity modeling to attention and reports improved language learning efficiency, downstream performance, and rule-based reasoning.

paragraphs: A model trained to favor particular answers may not be best suited to a test-time procedure that searches across many attempts. This paper examines pass@N, which measures whether at least one of N independent samples is correct. It shows that longer cross-entropy training can reduce this measure, creating a mismatch between the training objective and the later search strategy.

The authors explain the mismatch through overconfidence induced by cross-entropy training and experimentally test that explanation. They propose a modified loss that limits model confidence to better align learning with pass@N. The purpose is to improve the usefulness of multiple sampled attempts under the subsequent test-time compute strategy.

The method improves mathematical reasoning on MATH and MiniF2F in several evaluated settings. These include answers generated with or without chain-of-thought traces and theorem proving through proof-tree searches of different shapes. The findings support designing training objectives together with inference-time search: an objective that improves conventional training behavior can still be poorly aligned with the way a model will eventually be used.
neurips-2025-rethinking-fine-tuning-when.tldr: Limiting confidence during fine-tuning improves reported mathematical reasoning when test-time search uses multiple samples, addressing a mismatch with cross-entropy training.

paragraphs: Text watermarking aims to embed information that can help attribute generated content. Many methods require access to a model’s internal token scores or involve training, which limits their use with closed-source APIs. SAEMark proposes an inference-time approach that needs only black-box access and can embed personalized messages containing multiple bits.

The framework uses feature-based rejection sampling. Sparse autoencoders serve as deterministic feature extractors, and the resulting features guide which generated samples are accepted. This places the watermarking mechanism in sample selection: the method does not directly rewrite the outputs or manipulate the model’s logits. The authors also provide worst-case theory relating watermark accuracy to the available computational budget.

Experiments across four datasets report strong watermarking performance on English, Chinese, and code while preserving text quality. These results support applying the same framework across languages and domains. Its practical contribution is a way to carry personalized watermark information through black-box generation, with an explicit analysis of the relationship between computational effort and watermark accuracy.
neurips-2025-saemark-steering-personaliz.tldr: SAEMark embeds personalized multi-bit text watermarks through feature-based sample selection using only black-box model access.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can produce strong embeddings after contrastive fine-tuning, but the source of that strength is not fully understood. This paper argues that generative pretraining already aligns information from different modalities: the language decoder learns to use multimodal signals in a shared representation space to generate its outputs.

Analyses of representation anisotropy and kernel similarity provide empirical evidence for this latent alignment. On that basis, the authors treat contrastive learning as a lightweight refinement stage and introduce LCO-Embed, a language-centered embedding framework. Across multiple backbones and benchmarks, they report state-of-the-art performance across modalities, supporting the usefulness of building on alignment acquired during generation training.

The paper also identifies a positive scaling relationship between generative capability and representation quality after contrastive refinement. Its theoretical account connects generative quality to an upper bound on representation performance. On a low-resource visual-document retrieval task, continued generative pretraining before contrastive learning improves embedding potential. Together, these findings suggest that strengthening generation can be a productive route to better representations.
neurips-2025-scaling-language-centric-om.tldr: LCO-Embed builds on cross-modal alignment acquired during generative pretraining, linking stronger generation with better embeddings after contrastive refinement.

paragraphs: In predict-then-optimize systems, a model estimates unknown parameters that an optimizer uses to make decisions. Decision-focused learning trains those estimates for downstream decision quality, but repeatedly solving the optimization problem during loss evaluation can be expensive. This paper develops a training method that avoids that repeated solver use for linear optimization problems.

The method exploits the geometry of the feasible polytope. A candidate solution is optimal when its objective value is at least as good as those of its adjacent vertices. The proposed loss therefore compares the predicted objective value of the ground-truth optimal solution with values at its precomputed neighbors, turning a geometric optimality condition into a training signal.

This comparison directs the predictor toward parameters that favor the correct decision without solving a fresh optimization problem at every loss evaluation. Experiments report substantially lower computational cost while retaining high decision quality, with minimal degradation in solution quality. The approach’s significance lies in using the local structure around known optimal solutions to make decision-focused training more efficient.
neurips-2025-solver-free-decision-focuse.tldr: A neighbor-comparison loss uses linear optimization geometry to train decision-focused models without repeatedly calling a solver.

paragraphs: Iterative synthetic-data bootstrapping alternates between generating examples, filtering them with an external verifier, and fine-tuning on the accepted subset. As the model improves, the usefulness of spending resources at different iterations can change. This paper asks how a total generation and training budget should be distributed across that process to maximize final performance.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for comparing allocation policies. Within that framework, constant policies fail to converge with high probability, while policies that increase spending over iterations have theoretical advantages. Exponential growth receives particular attention, making the timing of computation a central part of the learning procedure rather than treating every iteration identically.

Experiments investigate image denoising with diffusion probabilistic models and mathematical reasoning with language models. Both polynomial and exponential growth policies consistently outperform constant policies in those tests, and exponential policies often behave more stably. The findings support allocating progressively larger resources as bootstrapping advances, with the empirical comparison complementing the theoretical analysis of how spending schedules affect learning.
neurips-2025-spend-wisely-maximizing-pos.tldr: Increasing generation and training budgets across bootstrapping iterations outperforms constant spending in reported experiments, with theoretical advantages for growing policies.

paragraphs: This paper attempts to bring visual understanding and image generation into one discrete semantic representation. Its Text-Aligned Tokenizer converts images into tokens using a codebook projected from a language model’s vocabulary. This makes the visual representation explicitly connected to the model’s textual vocabulary, supporting a shared space for processing both kinds of information.

The resulting multimodal model, Tar, uses an expanded vocabulary and a shared interface for cross-modal inputs and outputs. Scale-adaptive encoding and decoding balance computational efficiency with visual detail. To convert token representations back into images, the framework provides two complementary de-tokenizers: a fast autoregressive model and a diffusion-based model intended to support diverse decoding needs.

The authors also investigate pretraining tasks that strengthen the integration of modalities, reporting improvements in both understanding and generation. Across benchmarks, Tar matches or exceeds existing multimodal methods while converging faster and using training more efficiently. The findings support text-aligned visual tokens as a useful foundation for a model that both interprets and produces visual content.
neurips-2025-vision-as-a-dialect-unifyin.tldr: Tar uses text-aligned image tokens to unify visual understanding and generation, reporting competitive performance and improved training efficiency.
